title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
summary: The paper addresses that standard deep learning regression and classification do not capture model uncertainty, while Bayesian alternatives are computationally prohibitive. It casts dropout training in deep neural networks as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes, yielding MC dropout: T stochastic forward passes at test time to estimate predictive mean, variance, and log-likelihood. On UCI regression benchmarks it reports improved test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood over VI and PBP, e.g. Boston Housing RMSE 2.97 ±0.19 versus PBP 3.01 ±0.18 and VI 4.32 ±0.29.

match_target.why: Boston Housing is the smallest UCI regression dataset (506 points, 13 dimensions) and the 1-hidden-layer 50-unit dropout model is cheap to train; its Table 1 RMSE directly supports the paper's central claim that MC dropout improves predictive RMSE over VI and PBP.

tolerance.why: Rule 4: RMSE is unbounded. The paper reports a standard error over 20 splits (±0.19), not a std over repeated runs, so Rule 1 does not apply; 10% relative on 2.97 gives [2.673, 3.267].

requirements.stmt: At test time, collect T stochastic forward passes with dropout active and average them to form the predictive mean.
requirements.quote: In practice this is equivalent to performing T stochastic forward passes through the network and averaging the results.

requirements.stmt: Estimate predictive variance as the sample variance of the T stochastic forward passes plus inverse model precision τ^{-1} I_D.
requirements.quote: which equals the sample variance of T stochastic forward passes through the NN plus the inverse model precision.

requirements.stmt: Convert the prior length-scale l, weight decay λ, and keep probability to model precision via τ = p l^2 / (2 N λ).
For regression, compute predictive log-likelihood with eq. (8) using logsumexp over T stochastic forward passes and model precision τ.
requirements.quote: with a log-sum-exp of T terms and byt stochastic forward passes through the network.

requirements.stmt: Apply dropout before every weight layer in the network, following the paper's variational interpretation.
requirements.quote: with dropout applied before every weight layer

requirements.stmt: Use a single hidden layer with 50 hidden units for the UCI regression experiments.
Use dropout probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 for the small UCI regression network.
requirements.quote: We used dropout with probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 since the network size is very small

requirements.stmt: Train with Adam and mini-batches of size 32.
requirements.quote: Finally, we used mini-batches of size 32 and the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2014).

requirements.stmt: Run Bayesian optimisation over validation log-likelihood for 40 iterations to find τ, then retrain with optimal parameters for 10x more iterations.
requirements.quote: The BO runs used 40 iterations following the original setup, but after finding the optimal parameter values we used 10x more iterations

requirements.stmt: Set prior length-scale l to 10^-2 for most datasets based on data range.
requirements.quote: set the prior length-scale to 10−2 for most datasets based on the range of the data.

requirements.stmt: Average results over 20 random train/test splits for Boston Housing and most UCI datasets.
requirements.quote: All experiments were averaged on 20 random splits of the data

requirements.stmt: Compute test RMSE by averaging stochastic forward passes through the network at test time (MC dropout), not by standard weight averaging.
requirements.quote: Dropout’s RMSE in table 1 is given by averaging stochastic forward passes through the network following eq. (6) (MC dropout).
